\section[titulus, titulī]{titulus, titulī — a notice, a label; a title}

\label{lesson:LA-C164-titulus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to decide, then the Latin for to foresee.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: titulus, titulī}
\textbf{titulus, titulī} — \textquotedblleft{}a notice, a label; a title\textquotedblright{}. A shop or house could carry one by its door. The famous Pompeian doorway warning is a mosaic, but it reads like one: \textbf{Cavē canem.} — \textquotedblleft{}Beware of the dog.\textquotedblright{} English \emph{title} comes from it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{titulus, titulī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{titulus, titulī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to decide, then the Latin for to foresee, then say \emph{titulus, titulī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does titulus, titulī mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A notice, a label; a title\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis]{īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis — an inscription}

\label{lesson:LA-C164-inscriptio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to foresee, then the Latin for a notice.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis}
\textbf{īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}an inscription\textquotedblright{}. Read the stone: \textbf{SPQR} is \textbf{Senātus Populusque Rōmānus}, \textquotedblleft{}the Senate and People of Rome\textquotedblright{}. It is \textbf{in} + \textbf{scrībō}: writing cut into something.

  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for to foresee, then the Latin for a notice, then say \emph{īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis} again

\section[pretium, pretiī]{pretium, pretiī — a price}

\label{lesson:LA-C164-pretium}

Before the new one: say the Latin for a notice, then the Latin for an inscription.

\textbf{pretium, pretiī} — \textquotedblleft{}a price\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{Quantī cōnstat?} — \textquotedblleft{}How much does it cost?\textquotedblright{} English \emph{price} and \emph{precious} come from it.

\section[vēnālis, vēnāle]{vēnālis, vēnāle — for sale}

\label{lesson:LA-C164-venalis}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for an inscription, then the Latin for a price.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vēnālis, vēnāle}
\textbf{vēnālis, vēnāle} — \textquotedblleft{}for sale\textquotedblright{}. Read the sign: \textbf{Domus vēnālis.} — \textquotedblleft{}House for sale.\textquotedblright{} It comes from \textbf{vēnum}, \textquotedblleft{}sale\textquotedblright{}, like \textbf{vendō}, \textquotedblleft{}to sell\textquotedblright{}.

\section[merx, mercis]{merx, mercis — goods, merchandise}

\label{lesson:LA-C164-merx}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a price, then the Latin for for sale.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: merx, mercis}
\textbf{merx, mercis} — \textquotedblleft{}goods, merchandise\textquotedblright{}. What a shop sells: \textbf{mercēs} in the plural. That is not the same word as \textbf{mercēs, mercēdis}, \textquotedblleft{}wages\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{merchant} and \emph{commerce} come from it.

\section[(dialogue)]{Saying no and looking back — a first pass}

\label{lesson:LA-R164-first-pass-saying-no-and-looking-back}



\begin{quote}
Say the words for for sale and goods.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nothing, nobody, no, which, and not
  \item recently, the day before yesterday, once, before, to happen
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Nothing? (\textbf{nihil}.) Nobody? (\textbf{nēmō, nēminis}.) No? (\textbf{nūllus, nūlla, nūllum}.) Which? (\textbf{uter, utra, utrum}.) And not? (\textbf{neque}.) Recently? (\textbf{nūper}.) The day before yesterday? (\textbf{nudiustertius}.) Once? (\textbf{ōlim}.) Before? (\textbf{anteā}.) To happen? (\textbf{accidō, accidere}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(dialogue)]{Looking ahead and reading signs — a second pass}

\label{lesson:LA-R164-second-pass-looking-ahead-and-reading-signs}



\begin{quote}
Say the words for the day after tomorrow and afterwards.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the day after tomorrow, afterwards, a plan; advice, to decide, to foresee
  \item a notice, an inscription, a price, for sale, goods
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The day after tomorrow? (\textbf{perendiē}.) Afterwards? (\textbf{posteā}.) A plan; advice? (\textbf{cōnsilium, cōnsiliī}.) To decide? (\textbf{cōnstituō, cōnstituere}.) To foresee? (\textbf{prōvideō, prōvidēre}.) A notice? (\textbf{titulus, titulī}.) An inscription? (\textbf{īnscrīptiō, īnscrīptiōnis}.) A price? (\textbf{pretium, pretiī}.) For sale? (\textbf{vēnālis, vēnāle}.) Goods? (\textbf{merx, mercis}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
